major.name: International Studies - BA - Philosophy

items.text: Foreign language (four quarters of college-level language or equivalent proficiency). Students may also complete this requirement by demonstrating advanced language ability on a proficiency exam or by proof of native ability.

items.label: Philosophy Disciplinary Focus lower-division requirement
items.notes: IS majors must satisfy the following lower-division department requirement with a C– or better.

items.label: Cluster B: Philosophical Topics in Contemporary International Studies

items.notes: The remaining three courses will be at the student’s discretion.

requirement.label: Interdisciplinary Electives
requirement.notes: Three 4-unit, upper-division, nonlanguage courses chosen from the ISP Interdisciplinary Elective list. (Courses may not be from Disciplinary Focus department; those entries are omitted here.) MUS 111 counts ONLY when not on the U.S.; VIS 152 only when International in content; SOCI 189 must be preapproved by program adviser; rotating-topic courses by petition.

requirement.text: Regional Requirement: Of the eleven Disciplinary Focus and Interdisciplinary Elective courses (eight Disciplinary Focus and three Interdisciplinary Electives), three courses must concentrate on one country or region outside the United States.

narrative: All upper-division courses applied to the requirements of the major must be taken for a letter grade.
A 2.0 grade point average is required in the major, and students must earn at least a C– in each course counted for the major.
Subject to approval by the faculty director of the major, up to four courses taken through EAP/OAP will be accepted for credit toward the major.
INTL 100 is a prerequisite to INTL 101 and INTL 102. At least one quarter of university-level writing and sophomore status are prerequisites for INTL 100.
Disciplinary Focus and Interdisciplinary Elective courses must be 4-unit, upper-division, nonlanguage courses.

nodes.title: Analysis, Argument, and Real-World Problems
groups: Upper-Division Requirements: Core Courses: Core Courses
nodes.prereq_text: sophomore standing or above and completion of at least one quarter of a university-level writing course.

items.text: completion of at least one quarter of a university-level writing course

nodes.description: Focuses on developing skills in analytic reading and writing while using an interdisciplinary approach to asking and answering real-world questions. Lectures are topical and built around a series of readings that build in complexity and nuance; students work in an iterative process that builds toward a final policy memo project.

nodes.title: Culture and Society in International Perspective
groups: Upper-Division Requirements: Core Courses: Core Courses
nodes.prereq_text: completion of INTL 100 with a grade of C– or better.
nodes.description: Analysis of the cultural and social development of the modern era from the perspective of interaction among societies. Particular attention is paid to the definition, representation, and negotiation of social and cultural boundaries over time.

nodes.title: Economics, Politics, and International Change
groups: Upper-Division Requirements: Core Courses: Core Courses
nodes.prereq_text: completion of INTL 100 with a grade of C– or better.
nodes.description: Examination of the domestic and international sources of economic and political change. Topics include the rise of the nation-state, comparative economic development, authoritarian and democratic regimes, international and civil conflict, globalization and its domestic and international implications.

nodes.title: Introduction to Logic
groups: Lower-Division Requirements: Philosophy Disciplinary Focus lower-division requirement
nodes.description: Basic concepts and techniques in both informal and formal logic and reasoning, including a discussion of argument, inference, proof, and common fallacies, and an introduction to the syntax, semantics, and proof method in sentential (propositional) logic.

nodes.title: Philosophy and the Rise of Modern Science
Philosophy in the Americas
nodes.description: An exploration of central philosophical issues as they have been taken up in the diverse philosophical traditions of the Americas, such as indigenous philosophy, Latin American philosophy, American Pragmatism, and the Civil Rights movement, among others. Topics may include ethics, social and political philosophy, colonialism, philosophy of race and gender, environmentalism, and issues in philosophy of language.

nodes.title: Plato
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster A: History of Philosophy
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: A study of Socrates and/or Plato through major dialogues of Plato. Possible topics include the virtues and happiness; weakness of the will; political authority and democracy; the theory of Forms and sensible flux; immortality; relativism, skepticism, and knowledge. May be repeated for credit with change of content and approval of instructor. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Aristotle
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster A: History of Philosophy
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: A study of major issues in Aristotle’s works, such as the categories; form and matter; substance, essence, and accident; the soul; virtue, happiness, and politics. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Hellenistic Philosophy
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster A: History of Philosophy
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: A study of selected texts from the main schools of Hellenistic philosophy—Stoicism, Epicureanism, and Skepticism. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: The Rationalists
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: The major writings of one or more of the seventeenth-century rationalists—Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz. Topics include the existence of God, the mind-body problem, free will, the nature of knowledge, belief, and error. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Topics in Early Modern Philosophy
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: A study of one or more figures from seventeenth- and/or eighteenth-century philosophy, such as Bacon, Descartes, Hobbes, Cavendish, Conway, Spinoza, Locke, Malebranche, Leibniz, Astell, Berkeley, Du Chatelet, Hume, or Reid. The focus may be on particular texts or intellectual themes and traditions. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Kant
nodes.prereq_text: PHIL 32 or 33 or 104 or 105 or 111 or 112 or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: A study of selected portions of The Critique of Pure Reason and other theoretical writings and/or his major works in moral theory. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Hegel
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster A: History of Philosophy
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: A study of one or more of Hegel’s major works, in particular, The Phenomenology of Spirit and The Philosophy of Right. Readings and discussion may also include other figures in the Idealist tradition—such as Fichte, Hölderlin, and Schelling—and critics of the Idealist tradition—such as Marx and Kierkegaard. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Nineteenth-Century Philosophy
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: A study of one or more figures in nineteenth-century philosophy, such as Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Kierkegaard, Marx, Emerson, Thoreau, Goldman, Luxemburg, James, and Mill. The focus may be on particular figures or intellectual themes and traditions. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: History of Analytic Philosophy
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Central texts, figures, and traditions in analytic philosophy. Figures may include Frege, Russell, Wittgenstein, Carnap, Moore, Austin, Quine, and Anscombe. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: History of Philosophy: Ancient
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster A: History of Philosophy
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing and department stamp or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: An examination of ancient Greek philosophy, focusing on major works of Plato and Aristotle. PHIL 10, PHIL 111, and PHIL 112 should be taken in order.

nodes.title: History of Philosophy: Early Modern
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster A: History of Philosophy
nodes.prereq_text: PHIL 110, upper-division standing and department stamp or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: An examination of seventeenth- and eighteenth-century philosophy, focusing on major works of Descartes, Locke, and Hume. PHIL 110, PHIL 111, and PHIL 112 should be taken in order.

nodes.title: History of Philosophy: Late Modern
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster A: History of Philosophy
nodes.prereq_text: PHIL 111, upper-division standing and department stamp or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: An examination of late eighteenth and nineteenth-century philosophy, focusing on major works of Kant and Hegel. PHIL 110, PHIL 111, and PHIL 112 should be taken in order.

nodes.title: Philosophical Methods Seminar
nodes.prereq_text: open to philosophy majors only.
nodes.description: This course provides an introduction to the techniques of philosophical inquiry through detailed study of selected philosophical texts and through extensive training in philosophical writing based on those texts. Enrollment limited and restricted to majors; must be taken for letter grade.

nodes.title: Symbolic Logic I
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster C: Logic Requirement
nodes.prereq_text: PHIL 10 or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: The syntax, semantics, and proof-theory of first order monadic and polyadic predicate logic. In this course, we will learn how to determine whether arguments that can be represented in first order predicate logic are deductively valid, how to symbolize English arguments, the rules of a natural deduction system, how to apply those rules to determine the logical status of symbolized arguments, and how to use semantic methods for determining validity and invalidity. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Advanced Topics in Logic
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster C: Logic Requirement
nodes.prereq_text: PHIL 120 or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Topics vary from year to year. They include Metalogic (Mathematical Logic), Modal Logic, Foundations of Logic, Foundations of Set Theory, Gödel’s Incompleteness Theorems, and others.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Logic
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster C: Logic Requirement
nodes.prereq_text: PHIL 120 or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Philosophical issues underlying standard and nonstandard logics, the nature of logical knowledge, the relation between logic and mathematics, the revisability of logic, truth and logic, ontological commitment and ontological relativity, logical consequence, etc. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Mathematics
nodes.prereq_text: PHIL 120 or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: The character of logical and mathematical truth and knowledge; the relations between logic and mathematics; the significance of Gödel’s Incompleteness Theorem; Platonism, logicism, and more recent approaches. May be repeated for credit three times with change of content.

nodes.title: Probability and Decision Theory
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: A survey of theories of rational inference and rational choice, covering topics in probability and decision theory, formal epistemology, and statistics. This course provides an introduction to formal methods widely used in contemporary philosophy. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Topics in the History of Logic
nodes.prereq_text: PHIL 120 or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Problems and figures in history of logic. Subject matter varies, in some cases a single author or text (e.g., Aristotle, The Port Royal Logic, Leibniz, Kant, Frege, Tarski), in others a particular tradition or problem (e.g., Hilbert’s Program, intuitionism, quantification, logicism and psychologism, modality). May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Metaphysics
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Central problems in metaphysics, such as free will and determinism, the mind-body problem, personal identity, causation, primary and secondary qualities, the nature of universals, necessity, and identity.

nodes.title: Topics in Metaphysics
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: An in-depth study of some central problem, figure, or tradition in metaphysics. May be repeated for credit with change of content and approval of instructor. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Epistemology
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster B: Philosophical Topics in Contemporary International Studies
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Central problems in epistemology such as skepticism; a priori knowledge; knowledge of other minds; self-knowledge; the problem of induction; foundationalist, coherence, and causal theories of knowledge. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Language
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster B: Philosophical Topics in Contemporary International Studies
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Examination of contemporary debates about meaning, reference, truth, and thought. Topics include descriptional theories of reference, sense and reference, compositionality, truth, theories of meaning, vagueness, metaphor, and natural and formal languages. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Mind
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster B: Philosophical Topics in Contemporary International Studies
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Different conceptions of the nature of mind and its relation to the physical world. Topics include identity theories, functionalism, eliminative materialism, internalism and externalism, subjectivity, other minds, consciousness, self-knowledge, perception, memory, and imagination.

nodes.title: Moral Psychology
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster B: Philosophical Topics in Contemporary International Studies
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: The nature of action and psychological explanation. Topics include action individuation, reasons as causes, psychological laws, freedom and responsibility, weakness of will, self-deception, and the emotions.

nodes.title: Responsibility
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster B: Philosophical Topics in Contemporary International Studies
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: A study of the nature and significance of responsibility. Possible topics include freedom, determinism, and responsibility; moral luck; responsibility and reactive attitudes such as blame and forgiveness; responsibility and situationism; moral and criminal responsibility; responsibility and excuse; insanity and psychopathy, immaturity, addiction, provocation, and duress.

nodes.title: Global Justice
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster B: Philosophical Topics in Contemporary International Studies
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Social justice issues as they arise across the borders of nation-states. Topics may include nationalism and cosmopolitanism, theories of just war and just warfare, issues of migration and immigration, global distributive justice and fair trade, and international cooperation in the face of global problems such as climate change and human rights violations.

nodes.title: Free Will
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Investigation into the nature of free will, including arguments for and against its compatibility with a scientific picture of the world and competing accounts of the metaphysics of free will. Possible topics include disputes about the nature of free will; what it is for agents to cause actions; the nature of abilities or capacities to act; the relevance of neuroscience to accounts of free will; whether free will skepticism is a stable view; and experimental research on free will.

nodes.title: The Meaning of Life
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: This course considers whether human life has meaning, and, if so, what meaning it has and under what conditions such meaning may be secured. Negative proposals considered include that life is nothing but suffering, that it is absurd, that it has no meaning. Positive proposals considered include that meaning derives from free choices, from just being, from some passion, from something transcendent, or from human relationships or purposeless play or knowledge or achievement or morality.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Emotion
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: The nature, function, and value of emotion. Topics include theoretical approaches to defining (and distinguishing particular) emotions; the roles of emotions in structuring perception, cognition, and action; the rationality of emotion; morality and the emotions; emotions and mental/social well-being; and specific emotions such as fear or grief. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Perception
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: The nature and function of perception. Topics include theoretical approaches to defining (and distinguishing particular) perceptual modalities; informational interactions within and between these modalities, and between perception and thought; the roles of perception in justifying knowledge about the world and guiding both thought and action; and the nature of perceptible qualities (colors, sounds, smells, tastes). May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Science
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Central problems in philosophy of science, such as the nature of confirmation and explanation, the nature of scientific revolutions and progress, the unity of science, and realism and antirealism.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Physics
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Philosophical problems in the development of modern physics, such as the philosophy of space and time, the epistemology of geometry, the philosophical significance of Einstein’s theory of relativity, the interpretation of quantum mechanics, and the significance of modern cosmology. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Biology
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Philosophical problems in the biological sciences, such as the relation between biology and the physical sciences, the status and structure of evolutionary theory, and the role of biology in the social sciences. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Philosophy and the Environment
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster B: Philosophical Topics in Contemporary International Studies
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Investigation of ethical and epistemological questions concerning our relationship to the environment. Topics may include the value of nature, biodiversity, policy and science, and responsibility to future generations. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Psychology
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Philosophical issues raised by psychology, including the nature of psychological explanation, the role of nature versus nurture, free will and determinism, and the unity of the person. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Philosophy of the Cognitive Sciences
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Theoretical, empirical, methodological, and philosophical issues at work in the cognitive sciences (e.g., psychology, linguistics, neuroscience, artificial intelligence, and computer science), concerning things such as mental representation, consciousness, rationality, explanation, and nativism. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Neuroscience
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: An introduction to elementary neuroanatomy and neurophysiology and an examination of theoretical issues in cognitive neuroscience and their implications for traditional philosophical conceptions of the relation between mind and body, perception, consciousness, understanding, emotion, and the self. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Social Science
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Philosophical issues of method and substance in the social sciences, such as causal and interpretive models of explanation, structuralism and methodological individualism, value neutrality, and relativism. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Philosophy and Animals
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: An examination of one or more philosophical issues pertaining to animals. Topics will vary and may address animal ethics, animal minds, animals in the philosophy of science or conservation, metaphysical or epistemological questions related to animals, or the treatment of animals in a particular tradition or period in the history of philosophy. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Mexican Philosophy
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster A: History of Philosophy
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Introduction to Mexican philosophy with discussion of the work of such figures as Las Casas, Sor Juana Ines de la Cruz, Vasconcelos, Uranga, Zea, Villoro, Dussel, Hierro, Lara, and Hurtado. Topics may include historical movements, such as scholasticism, positivism, Mexican existentialism, and indigenous thought, as well as contemporary developments and the relationship to philosophy in the United States, Europe, and elsewhere. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Latinx Philosophy
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster A: History of Philosophy
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Philosophical issues surrounding Latina/o/x peoples, which may include debates about the nature, function, and stability of this identity; social and political issues, such as immigration, economics, racial politics, and justice; phenomenological and existential accounts of latinidad; Latina feminism; and the relationship of these concerns to other philosophical traditions.

nodes.title: Topics in Latin American and Latinx Philosophy
nodes.prereq_text: PHIL 35 or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: A study and in-depth analysis of one or more figures or themes in Latin American or Latina/o/x/e philosophy. The focus may be on particular topics (liberation, indigeneity, immigration, the idea of regional or ethno-philosophy), figures (for example, Sor Juana, Vasconcelos, Mariategui), or themes in historical or contemporary philosophy (such as Mexican existentialism, philosophy of liberation, Latina feminism). May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Topics in Chinese Philosophy
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster A: History of Philosophy
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: A study of one or more highly influential figures from Chinese philosophy, such as Confucius, Mozi, Mencius, Laozi, Zhuangzi, Xunzi, Han Feizi, and later Chinese thinkers. The focus may be on particular texts or intellectual themes and traditions. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Metaethics
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: An examination of foundational questions about morality, including issues such as ethical objectivity; the relation between science and ethics; metaphysical, epistemological, and semantic issues about ethics; moral expertise; moral conflict; moral motivation; morality and practical reason; and the rational authority of morality. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Ethical Theory
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster B: Philosophical Topics in Contemporary International Studies
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Systematic and/or historical perspectives on central issues in ethical theory such as deontic, contractualist, and consequentialist conceptions of morality; rights and special obligations; the role of happiness and virtue in morality; moral conflict; ethical objectivity and relativism; and the rational authority of morality. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Topics in the History of Ethics
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster A: History of Philosophy
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Central issues and texts in the history of ethics. Subject matter can vary, ranging from one philosopher (e.g., Confucius, Aristotle, Kant, or Mill) to a historical tradition (e.g., Greek ethics or the British moralists). May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Contemporary Moral Issues
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster B: Philosophical Topics in Contemporary International Studies
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: An examination of contemporary moral issues, such as abortion, euthanasia, war, affirmative action, and freedom of speech. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Biomedical Ethics
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster B: Philosophical Topics in Contemporary International Studies
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Moral issues in medicine and the biological sciences, such as patient’s rights and physician’s responsibilities, abortion and euthanasia, the distribution of health care, experimentation, and genetic intervention. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Technology and Human Values
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster B: Philosophical Topics in Contemporary International Studies
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Philosophical issues involved in the development of modern science, the growth of technology, and control of the natural environment. The interaction of science and technology with human nature and political and moral ideals.

nodes.title: Freedom, Equality, and the Law
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster B: Philosophical Topics in Contemporary International Studies
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Examination of freedom and equality under the US Constitution, focusing on Supreme Court cases concerning discrimination on grounds of race, ethnic background, gender, undocumented status, wealth, and sexual orientation, and cases regarding contraceptives, abortion, interracial marriage, polygamy, and same-sex marriage.

nodes.title: Classics in Political Philosophy
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster A: History of Philosophy
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Central issues about the justification, proper functions, and limits of the state through classic texts in the history of political philosophy by figures such as Plato, Aristotle, Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, Marx, and Arendt. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Contemporary Political Philosophy
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster B: Philosophical Topics in Contemporary International Studies
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Different perspectives on central issues in contemporary political philosophy, such as the nature of state authority and political obligation, the limits of government and individual liberty, liberalism and its critics, equality and distributive justice. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Law
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: A study of issues in analytical jurisprudence such as the nature of law, the relation between law and morality, and the nature of legal interpretation and issues in normative jurisprudence such as the justification of punishment, paternalism and privacy, freedom of expression, and affirmative action. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Feminism and Philosophy
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster A: History of Philosophy
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Philosophical examination of core concepts and theses in feminism, feminist philosophy, and critiques of traditional philosophical approaches to morality, politics, and science, from a feminist perspective. May also treat the historical development of feminist philosophy and its critiques. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Philosophy and Race
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster B: Philosophical Topics in Contemporary International Studies
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: A philosophical investigation of the topics of race and racism. The role of “race” in ordinary speech. The ethics of racial discourse. Anthropological and biological conceptions of race. The social and political significance of racial categories. Post-racialist conceptions of race. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Topics in Philosophy of Law
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: An in-depth analysis of one or more issues in philosophy of law. Topics might include legal positivism and natural law, legal and constitutional interpretation, judicial review within a constitutional democracy, First Amendment jurisprudence, substantive due process and equal protection, the limits of the criminal law, responsibility and punishment, psychiatry and the law, and the moral foundations of civil law. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Topics in Political Philosophy
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: An in-depth analysis of a central problem, figure, or tradition in political philosophy. Topics may include minority rights, war and peace, political philosophy as it pertains to animals or the environment, immigration, ideal vs. non-ideal theory, or a detailed examination of a contemporary thinker or school of political thought. Content may vary. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Topics in Bioethics
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster B: Philosophical Topics in Contemporary International Studies
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: An in-depth exploration of an issue in bioethics. Topics will vary, and may include the ethics of genetic engineering, mental capacity and genuinely informed consent, the just distribution of health care, the ethics of geo-engineering, and the ethics of climate change and health. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Data Ethics
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: A survey of ethical issues arising in the collection, storage, analysis, consolidation, and application of data. Topics may include data as property and public resource, privacy and surveillance, data and discrimination, algorithms and fairness, and data regulation.

nodes.title: Aesthetics
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Central issues in philosophical aesthetics such as the nature of art and aesthetic experience, the grounds of artistic interpretation and evaluation, artistic representation, and the role of the arts in education, culture, and politics. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Culture
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: This course examines the nature of culture, its significance, and its varied meanings. Topics may include case studies of culture’s relationship to psychology, politics, media, religion, and the arts. Course may include discussion of related questions concerning culture and race, class, nationalism, sexuality, and gender. Contemporary and classical readings, drawing from philosophy, anthropology, sociology, literature, religion, and related fields.

nodes.title: Philosophy and Literature
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: A study of philosophical themes contained in selected fiction, drama, or poetry, and the philosophical issues that arise in the interpretation, appreciation, and criticism of literature. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Topics in German Philosophy Translation—Intermediate
nodes.prereq_text: consent of instructor and preauthorization.
nodes.description: Careful, line-by-line translation of passages of intermediate difficulty from German philosophical texts, both classic (Kant, Fichte, Hegel, Schopenhauer) and contemporary (Heidegger, Wittgenstein, Habermas). P/NP grades only. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content. LIGM 1D or equivalent level of study recommended.

nodes.title: Topics in German Philosophy Translation—Advanced
nodes.prereq_text: consent of instructor or completion of PHIL 178.
nodes.description: Continuation of PHIL 178 in the careful, line-by-line translation of passages of advanced difficulty from German philosophical texts, both classic (Kant, Fichte, Hegel, Schopenhauer) and contemporary (Heidegger, Wittgenstein, Habermas). May be repeated for credit three times with change of content.

nodes.title: Phenomenology
groups: Disciplinary Focus: Cluster A: History of Philosophy
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: An examination of the phenomenological tradition through the works of its major classical and/or contemporary representatives. Authors studied will vary and may include Brentano, Husserl, Heidegger, Stein, Merleau-Ponty, Levinas, and Irigaray. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Existentialism
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Classical texts and issues of existentialism. Authors studied will vary and may include Nietzsche, Kierkegaard, Heidegger, Sartre, de Beauvoir, and Fanon. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Topics in Continental Philosophy
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: The focus will be on a leading movement in continental philosophy (e.g., the critical theory of the Frankfurt school, structuralism and deconstruction, postmodernism) or some particular issue that has figured in these traditions (e.g., freedom, subjectivity, historicity, authenticity). May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Philosophy and Film
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: This course may include topics in the philosophy of film, such as the nature of the cinematic medium, the aesthetic qualities of film, when film is art, how film is different from other artistic forms, the role of emotion, imagination, and thought in our experience of films, and why we enjoy horror and tragic movies. It may also discuss the philosophy in film by exploring how cinema engages with topics such as agency, responsibility, personal identity, justice, happiness, love, gender, etc. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Religion
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: A general introduction to the philosophy of religion through the study of classical and/or contemporary texts. Among the issues to be discussed are the existence and nature of God, the problem of evil, the existence of miracles, the relation between reason and revelation, and the nature of religious language. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Authoritarianism
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: This course analyzes the nature of authoritarianism, how it operates, what its consequences are, and what it justifies in response, by drawing from political philosophy, normative ethics, epistemology, legal philosophy, philosophy of psychology, and social philosophy. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

nodes.title: Applied Ethics
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing and consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Intensive application of ethics through contemporary moral dilemmas focused on developing oral and presentation skills in philosophy. Students will have the opportunity to join the department’s Ethics Bowl team for an annual national competition series. May be repeated for credit eight times with change of content.

nodes.title: Philosophy Honors
nodes.prereq_text: department approval; consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Independent study by special arrangement with and under the supervision of a faculty member, including a proposal for the honors essay. An IP grade will be awarded at the end of this quarter; a final grade will be given for both quarters at the end of 191B.

nodes.title: The Honors Essay
nodes.prereq_text: consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Continuation of 191A: independent study by special arrangement with and under the supervision of a faculty member, leading to the completion of the honors essay. A letter grade for both 191A and 191B will be given at the end of this quarter.

nodes.title: Pedagogy and Learning Apprenticeship
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing and consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Under the supervision of an instructor, undergraduate students gain teaching experience through practical experiences in course management and effective teaching methods. Pedagogy and learning apprentices must have a minimum overall grade point average of 3.0. A student may not apprentice more than once for the same course for credit or for more than one course in the same quarter. May be repeated for credit two times.

nodes.title: Directed Individual Study
nodes.prereq_text: consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Directed individual study by special arrangement with and under the supervision of a faculty member. (P/NP grades only.) May be repeated for credit four times with change of content and approval of instructor.
